title: CDNs
concept: A content delivery network keeps copies of content on servers spread close to users, so most requests are answered nearby instead of crossing the internet to the origin server. A CDN has two jobs: deciding what to keep at each edge when disk space is limited, and making the misses that still go back to the origin as cheap as possible.

points: A CDN keeps copies of content on servers close to users, so most requests are answered nearby instead of at the origin.
It has two jobs: deciding what each edge keeps when disk space is limited, and making the misses that still reach the origin cheap.
Cloudflare found a miss costs more than the trip to the origin, because setting up the connection counts, so connection reuse matters.
Netflix owns its catalog and can predict demand, so it fills caches ahead of time instead of waiting for misses.

figures.label: 160x fewer new connections to one customer's origins
around 1,200 files stored for one episode of The Crown

prerequisiteReasons.dns: CDNs take from DNS the way a user's request is pointed at a nearby server, which is how each user lands on a close edge.
prerequisiteReasons.caching: CDNs take from caching the hit, the miss and the fill, applied to many edge copies that sit in front of one origin.

posts.title: How we built Pingora, the proxy that connects Cloudflare to the Internet

digest.problem: This post covers the link between a CDN and the origin servers behind it, the path every cache miss takes, not edge caching itself. Cloudflare's proxy for that link was built on NGINX, where each worker process keeps its own pool of open connections to origins. Adding workers to handle more traffic split connections into more, smaller pools, so fewer requests found an open connection to reuse, and each new connection meant another TCP and TLS handshake before the first byte. A request was also stuck on one worker, so slow work on one request held up others, and the code was hard to extend.
digest.constraints: The proxy has to handle millions of requests per second, and it sees plenty of malformed or non-standard HTTP from across the internet, including status codes outside the official range, which it must pass through rather than reject. NGINX is written in C, where memory bugs are easy to make, and its scripting layer, Lua, is slower and has no type checking.

walkthrough.explanation: Cloudflare compared forking NGINX, moving to another proxy such as Envoy, and writing its own, and chose to build despite the highest upfront cost.
Rust gives performance close to C with memory safety.

Cloudflare must accept non-compliant HTTP traffic, such as status codes above 599, and wanted flexibility, so it wrote its own permissive HTTP library instead of using an off-the-shelf one such as hyper.
All threads share one pool of origin connections, so any request can reuse any open connection.
Idle threads take work from busy ones, so one slow request no longer blocks a whole worker's queue.
Teams plug custom logic into defined stages of a request, keeping product features separate from the core proxy.

walkthrough.step: Serve every trip to the origin
walkthrough.explanation: Pingora handles almost every request that must reach an origin, including cache misses, and reuses pooled connections to skip handshakes.

tradeoffs.chosen: A new proxy in Rust, using threads that share one connection pool, a custom HTTP library, and pluggable request phases.
tradeoffs.rejected: Forking NGINX, adopting a third-party proxy such as Envoy, writing in C or Lua, and keeping separate processes.
tradeoffs.why: The limits were in NGINX's process model, not its code speed: the old service already handled requests in under a millisecond, and the latency gains came from reusing connections. A fork would need that model rebuilt, and another proxy could hit the same walls within a few years. Building cost the most upfront but removed the constraint.

digest.failures: Cloudflare has to accept non-standard HTTP traffic, such as status codes above 599, and chose to write its own HTTP library for the flexibility. The hyper library did later accept that change. Across a few hundred trillion requests, Cloudflare says it has yet to see a crash caused by Pingora's service code. The rare crashes it did see led to a Linux kernel bug, and hardware issues on a few machines had in the past made rare software memory bugs nearly impossible to rule out.
digest.takeaways: For a CDN, the cost of a miss is not only the trip to the origin but setting up the connection for it, and Cloudflare called poor connection reuse its most critical problem. For latency, architecture, here shared pools instead of per-process ones, mattered more than faster code. Replace a foundation when working around it costs more than rebuilding it.

posts.title: Content Popularity for Open Connect
posts.ageNote: From 2017. The idea it teaches, deciding from predicted popularity what each edge keeps and pushing it there ahead of demand, is still how Netflix describes its CDN: its 2025 post on classifying cache misses points back to this one for how content is placed. Hardware figures such as 100 Gbps and 200 TB may have changed.

stillCitedBy.title: Driving Content Delivery Efficiency Through Classifying Cache Misses

digest.problem: This post covers edge placement: deciding what each edge server keeps. Netflix's CDN, Open Connect, puts its own servers inside internet providers' and exchange points' data centers, but many clusters near viewers do not have room for the whole catalog. So Netflix decides in advance, from predicted popularity, which files each cluster holds, instead of caching whatever happens to be requested.
digest.constraints: Each server has fixed disk space, and every title is many files: each combination of encoding profile, bitrate and language is stored separately, around 1,200 files for one episode of The Crown. Updates are downloaded off-peak, and every changed file costs providers and Netflix bandwidth. Servers fail, and popularity can spike without warning.

walkthrough.explanation: Popularity is how many times something is watched: bytes streamed divided by the file's size.
History over several days is smoothed, because reacting to one day's swings would churn content needlessly. New titles start from forecasts, marketing plans, and sometimes a human pinning them high.
Ranking each file on its own keeps unpopular bitrates of a popular title off scarce disk. Moving to this in 2016 gave the same caching efficiency with half the storage.
Popularity is computed per region, since viewers in one country tend to watch similar things.
At very busy sites, the most popular files go to high-throughput servers and the long tail to high-capacity storage servers.

Within a cluster, a file is stored on a number of servers roughly proportional to its popularity, assigned with consistent hashing, so load evens out and a failed server's traffic stays in the cluster.
Caching efficiency, the share of a cluster's traffic it serves itself, and content churn, how much has to change each day.

tradeoffs.chosen: Push content ahead of demand based on predicted, smoothed popularity, ranked per file and per region, with several copies of popular files spread by consistent hashing.
tradeoffs.rejected: Ranking whole titles, predicting from yesterday alone, and keeping a single copy of each file.
tradeoffs.why: Title ranking stores unpopular bitrates next to popular ones and wastes disk. One day of history reacts to noise and churns content. A single copy of a very popular file can overwhelm its server while others sit idle, though the post says routing by network proximity and keeping popular files in memory make this less pronounced for Netflix. Extra copies also even out traffic between servers and keep a failed server's traffic in the cluster. Splitting big files into several copies is like balancing pebbles instead of rocks.

digest.failures: The post describes no incident. It designs against three problems: uneven load when a popular file sits on one server, a server failure pushing its traffic to more distant sites, and sudden popularity spikes, which is why some mid-popularity content gets extra copies as insurance.
digest.takeaways: Netflix owns the catalog and can predict demand, so it fills caches ahead of time instead of waiting for requests. Choose the unit you rank and store carefully, since finer units saved half the storage here. Consistent hashing places the copies within a cluster, which ties this post to the Consistent Hashing topic.

glossary.definition: A CDN server close to users, which answers requests from its cache when it can.
The customer's own server, which holds the original content and is asked when the edge does not have it.
A request the edge cannot answer from its cache, so it goes back to the origin.
Sending a new request over an already open connection, skipping the setup handshakes.
The exchange that sets up an encrypted connection; it costs extra round trips before any data moves.
How long a client waits between sending a request and receiving the first byte of the answer.
Copying content to edge servers ahead of demand, based on predictions, instead of on the first request.
The share of a cluster's traffic that it serves from its own copies.
How much content has to be replaced on the edge each day.

mistakes: Judging a CDN only by its cache hit rate. Misses still go to the origin, and how cheaply they get there, including whether a connection is already open, decides much of the latency users see.
Giving each worker process its own pool of origin connections. Every worker you add splits the pool further, so connection reuse falls exactly when traffic grows.
Assuming faster code fixes slow misses. Cloudflare's old proxy already handled requests in under a millisecond; the delay came from new connections and their handshakes.
comparison:
The two posts cover different halves of a CDN and do not compete.

Netflix's covers edge placement: deciding ahead of time, from predicted popularity, which files each edge cluster keeps and how many copies, so content is served over the shortest network path possible. Cloudflare's Pingora covers the origin link: what happens on a miss, when the edge has to fetch from the customer's server, and how sharing connection pools makes that trip cheaper.

Netflix can predict demand for a catalog it owns and push files off-peak; Our own reading, not stated in either post: a CDN serving other people's sites cannot predict demand as well, so cheap misses matter more.

why.outcome: After this you can explain why serving content from one place is slow for most users, and what a CDN changes.
why.body:
A server in one data center is far from most of its users. Every request crosses the internet, and every new connection pays for handshakes before the first byte arrives. For a global audience, distance alone makes the site slow, and every request lands on the same origin servers.

A content delivery network keeps copies of content on servers spread close to users, so most requests are answered nearby. It is caching applied across the whole internet, with the same costs: limited room at each location, and misses that still have to go back to the origin.

mentalModel.outcome: After this you can picture where a request is answered and what happens on a miss.
mentalModel.body:
Picture many small caches, called edges, spread around the world, all in front of one origin that holds the real copy. DNS sends each user to a nearby edge. If the edge has the file, a hit, it answers at once over a short distance.

A CDN has two separate jobs. The first is deciding what each edge keeps, since no edge has room for everything. The second is making misses cheap, because whatever the edge does not hold has to be fetched from the origin, ideally over a connection that is already open.

howItWorks.outcome: After this you can walk through a CDN request from lookup to response, hit or miss.

steps.explanation: The user's DNS lookup returns the address of an edge close to them.
The edge looks for the file. A hit is served from there, which is the fast path.
On a miss, the edge requests the file from the origin, ideally reusing an open connection to skip TCP and TLS handshakes.
The edge keeps the file for later requests and returns it to the user.
With limited disk, the edge either keeps what was recently requested or is filled ahead of time with what is predicted to be popular.

workedExample.outcome: After this you can follow both halves of a CDN in real systems: placing content and making misses cheap.

steps.explanation: In a 2017 post, Netflix described how its Open Connect CDN decides in advance which files each edge cluster keeps, instead of waiting for requests.

One episode of The Crown is around 1,200 files, one per encoding, bitrate and language. Ranking each file separately kept unpopular bitrates off scarce disk and, from 2016, gave the same efficiency with half the storage.
Popular files are stored on several servers in a cluster, so no single server is overwhelmed.

Cloudflare's old origin proxy, built on NGINX, gave each worker process its own connection pool. More workers meant smaller pools, so fewer requests found an open connection and more paid for handshakes.

Its replacement, Pingora, uses threads sharing one pool. For one major customer, connection reuse went from 87.1% to 99.92%. Across all traffic, median and p95 time to first byte fell by 5 ms and 80 ms.

lesson.checkOutcome: After this you can tell whether you understood the concept before reading the posts.

quiz.question: What makes a CDN fast for most users?
options: A faster origin server that can answer every distant request in less time
Copies of content on servers close to them
Compressing every file twice so each response is smaller on the wire
quiz.why: Most requests are answered nearby instead of crossing the internet to the origin.
wrong: The origin is still far away; the edge avoids the trip.
Compression helps, but distance is the main cost a CDN removes.

quiz.question: What are a CDN's two jobs?
options: Encrypting traffic and storing passwords for the sites it serves, so origins need not
Replacing DNS and the origin, so that sites no longer need servers of their own
Deciding what each edge keeps, and making misses to the origin cheap
quiz.why: Edges have limited room, and whatever they do not hold must be fetched from the origin.
wrong: Those are not what a CDN is for.
A CDN relies on DNS and sits in front of the origin.

quiz.question: On a miss, why does reusing an open connection to the origin matter?
options: It skips TCP and TLS handshakes before the first byte
It makes the file smaller because the connection compresses what it carries
It turns the miss into a hit, since the origin now remembers the connection
quiz.why: Each new connection costs round trips; reuse removes them.
wrong: It is still a miss, just a cheaper one.

quiz.question: Each worker process keeps its own origin connection pool. You add workers. What happens to connection reuse?
options: It falls, because the pool is split into smaller pools
It rises, because more workers means more open connections to reuse
Nothing changes, because every worker already reuses connections the same way
quiz.why: Smaller pools mean fewer requests find an open connection, just when traffic grows.
wrong: Each worker has its own pool, so the split matters.

quiz.question: Why might a CDN rank and store individual files instead of whole titles?
options: So unpopular versions of a popular title do not take up scarce disk
To make files load in order
quiz.why: Finer units let only the popular bitrates and languages stay at the edge.
wrong: Titles can be cached; it is just wasteful.

quiz.question: How does a user get sent to a nearby edge?
options: Through the DNS answer for the site's name
quiz.why: The CDN uses the DNS lookup to return a nearby edge's address.
wrong: That would still send every first request to the origin.
Browsers use the address DNS returns.

lesson.postsOutcome: After this you can describe how two companies handled the two halves of a CDN: placing content and making misses cheap.
lesson.differOutcome: After this you can explain when to fill caches ahead of demand and when to make misses cheaper.
lesson.exercisesOutcome: After this you can apply the concept to a slow site, design a CDN, and plan for ten times the scale.

exercises.prompt: Your CDN reports a 95% hit rate, yet users on uncached pages see slow first bytes. Where do you look?
exercises.answer: At the miss path: how often a miss finds an open connection to the origin, and how many new TCP and TLS handshakes it pays for. Share connection pools so reuse stays high as traffic grows.
exercises.tradeoffs: Larger shared pools mean more connections held open to origins and more shared state in the proxy.
wrongAnswers: Judging the CDN on hit rate alone.
Assuming faster proxy code will fix slow misses.
Adding workers that each keep a private pool.

exercises.prompt: Design how a video service decides what each edge cluster holds.
exercises.answer: Predict popularity per region from several days of smoothed history plus forecasts for new titles, rank individual files rather than titles, and push them off-peak. Store popular files on several servers in the cluster, and track both caching efficiency and daily churn.
exercises.tradeoffs: Prediction can miss sudden spikes, so keep extra copies of mid-popularity content; pushing off-peak costs bandwidth.
wrongAnswers: Predicting from yesterday alone, which churns content.
Keeping a single copy of a very popular file.

exercises.prompt: Traffic grows ten times, mostly to content you cannot predict, such as customers' websites. What changes?
exercises.answer: You cannot place content ahead of time, so misses dominate. Make the miss path cheap with shared connection pools and work stealing, so one slow request does not block others, and size edge caches for recently requested content.
exercises.tradeoffs: Rebuilding the proxy is expensive up front; a shared pool adds coordination between threads.
wrongAnswers: Relying on prediction for content you do not control.
Scaling with more processes that each split the pool.

next.outcome: After this you can pick the next topic that builds on this one.
next.body: Inside each Netflix cluster, copies of popular files are spread across servers with consistent hashing. If you have not read it yet, Consistent Hashing explains how many servers agree on where each key lives, and Sharding builds on it for databases.
